There is no game quite like this one. It is an open-world crafting survival game with a premade map that takes place in an enclosed space. No procedurally generated map, no endless expanse of various biomes. Instead, you get a tightly curated, handcrafted world like Grounded or Subnautica. That’s great for atmosphere, but unlike those games, this one take place in an enclosed space.

The first time you visit a new sector, there are various routes you can take to reach your objective, but they’re usually long and tedious. The more you explore, the more shortcuts you unlock, and this is something you can’t really find in other survival crafting games. It feels genuinely rewarding and gives you a real sense of progression, similar to unlocking shortcuts in Souls games. You don’t have to go through all that trouble again.

As you progress through the game, each sector is affected by a hazardous weather event. For example, there might be fog that limits your vision, radioactive clouds, and other environmental hazards. These effects will eventually go away on their own, but it takes time. What you need to do is backtrack to one of the previous sectors and push a button to mitigate these weather effects. This lets you make use of the aforementioned shortcuts even after you’ve finished the area and moved several sectors ahead. Whoever designed this mechanic deserves an award.

The fact that you cannot build any structures in this game should be a cardinal sin, but it fits the theme so well. You’re forced to establish a base in some random nook of the facility because you’re constantly hiding from threats. The facility itself works against you. You feel like you’re somewhere you don’t belong.

I could talk for hours about why an enclosed space like this works so well for a survival crafting game. I mean, the game simulates a day-night cycle by having the entire facility shut down at night to save power. Walking around during the night feels incredibly atmospheric. It’s like exploring a school or workplace after hours.

There’s a lot more to talk about: the fact that this game is basically an SCP game, the portal worlds full of bizarre and terrifying things, the god-tier QoL features, the friggin’ Half-Life 1 aesthetic, the marketing campaign, the way the game keeps up the pace by making sleeping fun through minigames, the monsters, the progression system, the story, the weapons, and the upgrade system.

Holy mother of mercy, I’ve played a lot of great survival games before, but this… this is it.

Abiotic Factor has genuinely entered my top five of all time at this point. The crafting and progression is fun and intuitive - getting wood and metal from coffee tables and computers, instead of trees and ore veins, keeps the survival-crafter aspect fresh and fun. You'll fight with crossbows made out of rulers and telephone cords. You'll scavenge food and water from the various cafeterias and break rooms. You'll find a quaint little broom closet by the monorail depot and make it your home, decorating it with all the furniture, plants and paintings your scrawny lil' scientist can carry. All in an attempt to survive your first day on the job.

I could gush about this game all day. A love letter to fans of unique experiences, full of interesting and varied locations, portal travel, interdimensional creatures and so much more. I've played with friends and solo and can safely say it feels great either way, though experiencing the delights/thrills/horrors with a pal is always a good time. The developers are actively updating the game and communicating with the fanbase. I just... Seriously, ya'll. Play this game. I'm hard pressed to find a comparable experience to this one and I'll continue playing as it's updated.

A+++, Gold Star, See Me After Class (for more gold stars)

Imaginez un mélange entre Half-Life 1, la SCP Foundation et un jeu de survie/construction de base comme Grounded, pour citer un exemple. À la différence près que vous n'incarnez pas Gordon Freeman, mais un scientifique lambda essayant simplement de survivre au milieu du chaos, le tout avec une identité unique grâce à son univers rempli d'anomalies, de créatures étranges et d'expériences qui tournent mal.

Que ce soit en solo ou en coop, la progression est très satisfaisante, l'exploration donne toujours envie d'aller voir ce qui se cache derrière la prochaine porte, et l'humour du jeu fonctionne très bien sans casser l'ambiance. (Coucou Abe et Janet !)

115 heures plus tard, je continue à prendre du plaisir à y jouer. Si vous aimez la survie, l'univers SCP et l'ambiance Half-Life, foncez.

Possibly one of the best survival crafting games out there. Perfectly captures the sort of liminal retrofuturistic vibe of half-life 1, while delivering a compelling world and satisfying gameplay loops reminiscent of the SCP stories and survival games like The Forest. The later stages of the game host some of the most interesting and sprawling environments, but are sadly lacking the sheer density of content found in the earlier sectors--which is mostly a testament to how much Deepfield manages to pack into the intimate office spaces and research labs of the GATE facility. I am sure the late game will be expanded on significantly in the coming updates, as the developers have been so proactive about responding to community feedback post-release that it feels like multiple of my comments have been personally addressed in the recent and upcoming updates.

Full disclaimer: My friends who have bought the game quickly became frustrated because they did not care to speak to any of the NPCs, look at the computers, or follow the given quests. They quit before leaving the first section. The world is the main draw; you may not enjoy the game if you're not prepared to immerse yourself in it.
